items.text: Doesn't the impossibility of a perfect silicon neuron replacement fully collapse Chalmers's neural-replacement argument for substrate independence?
Isn't insisting that life matters for consciousness just another form of the exceptionalism bias the author warns against?
If simulation never amounts to instantiation, how can Bostrom's simulation hypothesis about our own universe still hold up?
If human biases explain most claims of AI consciousness, why does the author still admit conscious AI isn't entirely ruled out?
Why worry more about consciousness accidentally emerging in brain organoids than in the latest LLMs?
Why does it matter so much to separate actually conscious AI from merely conscious-seeming AI when deciding on rights?
If our sense of AI consciousness is as involuntary as a visual illusion, can arguments like this one actually change how we treat these systems?
Given no definitive test for consciousness exists, how can the author be so sure creating conscious AI would be an ethical disaster?
Since humans have a bad record of denying moral status to animals and other humans, isn't withholding it from AI repeating that mistake?
